title: Polyamine metabolism as a regulator of cellular and organismal aging

sections.abstract:
Polyamines - putrescine, spermidine, and spermine - are ubiquitous cationic molecules that are essential for cellular proliferation and homeostasis. Their intracellular concentrations decline with age, contributing to physiological and cognitive deterioration. Recent studies have revealed that spermidine supplementation extends lifespan and improves cognitive and cardiac function in various model organisms, suggesting that maintaining polyamine balance has anti-aging potential. Polyamine metabolism is tightly regulated through biosynthesis, degradation, and transport; however, age-associated upregulation of spermine oxidase (SMOX) and accumulation of its toxic byproduct acrolein promote oxidative damage and cellular senescence. Suppressing SMOX activity or polyamine degradation attenuates senescence markers and DNA damage, highlighting spermine catabolism as a therapeutic target. Polyamines also modulate epigenetic regulation, including DNA methylation and histone acetylation, thereby influencing gene expression and chromatin structure during aging. Moreover, polyamine-dependent hypusination of eIF5A sustains protein synthesis in senescent cells. These multifaceted actions indicate that polyamine metabolism integrates redox control, translational regulation, epigenetic maintenance and autophagy to determine cellular and organismal longevity. While animal studies demonstrate clear anti-aging effects of spermidine and spermine, human clinical evidence remains limited, with variable outcomes likely due to bioavailability and metabolic conversion. Future strategies combining dietary or probiotic polyamine enhancement, enzyme-targeted inhibitors, and personalized metabolic interventions hold promise for extending healthspan. Collectively, maintaining optimal polyamine homeostasis emerges as a key approach to counteract aging and age-related diseases.

Keywords: Aging, Senescence, Spermine oxidase, Polyamine metabolism, Translational regulation, Epigenetic regulation, Autophagy
sections.introduction:
Polyamines are essential low-molecular-weight cationic compounds found in almost all living organisms (Michael 2016 ). In mammals, putrescine, spermidine, and spermine are the primary polyamines. Polyamines bind to nucleic acids and proteins to promote cell proliferation and support physiological functions through mechanisms such as mRNA translation (Watanabe et al. 1991 ; Miyamoto et al. 1993 ; Igarashi and Kashiwagi 2000 ). However, polyamine concentrations in most tissues decline with aging, and this reduction has been reported to contribute to physical and cognitive decline (Nishimura et al. 2006 ; Pekar et al. 2020 ). Indeed, studies in aged mice, rats and Drosophila have demonstrated that polyamine supplementation, particularly with spermidine, restores cognitive function and extends lifespan (Eisenberg et al. 2009 , 2016 ; Gupta et al. 2013 ; Yue et al. 2017 ; Schroeder et al. 2021 ). In humans, spermidine supplementation also shows potential to improve cognitive decline and immune function impairment in the elderly (Schroeder et al. 2021 ). Conversely, the relationship between spermine degradation and cellular aging has also been highlighted in recent years (Uemura et al. 2020 , 2023 ). These findings suggest that age-related changes in polyamine metabolism contribute to aging, and that maintaining polyamine metabolic balance may contribute to anti-aging. However, despite strong evidence from animal models, human trials show mixed results due to variability in bioavailability, metabolism, and baseline polyamine status. This underscores the need for deeper understanding of tissue-specific regulation and more rigorous clinical studies.

This review summarizes current insights into polyamine metabolism and its roles in senescence, epigenetic regulation, and physiological aging, and evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting polyamine pathways to promote healthy aging.
sections.conclusion:
Polyamine metabolism is increasingly recognized as a central regulator of cellular and organismal aging. Age-associated declines in polyamines promote epigenetic instability, oxidative stress, and senescence, whereas supplementation or inhibition of catabolism can reverse these molecular abnormalities. Spermidine acts through multiple mechanisms—including autophagy induction, chromatin regulation, and mitochondrial maintenance—to extend lifespan and improve organ function in animal models (Gupta et al. 2013 ; Eisenberg et al. 2016 ; Kiechl et al. 2018 ; Madeo et al. 2018 ; Wang et al. 2020 ; Messerer et al. 2021 ).

Despite promising preclinical evidence, translation to humans remains challenging due to variability in metabolism and limited long-term clinical data. Notably, several clinical trials investigating spermidine supplementation are currently ongoing, as documented in ClinicalTrials.gov. Future studies should focus on personalized approaches that account for individual polyamine status, optimized delivery strategies that enhance bioavailability, and safety evaluation in populations at risk for cancer. Integrated interventions targeting polyamine metabolism alongside other aging pathways may ultimately provide effective strategies to extend human healthspan.
